paras: The killing of Jerry Johnson took place near Farmington, Tennessee, where the bullet-riddled body of Johnson, a Black man, was found on August 27, 1895. He had been warned days earlier to leave over an alleged improper proposal to a young girl, and wire reports said he was supposed to have been killed by a mob. Northern and western weeklies later reduced the story to a one-line item stating that he had been lynched for an insulting proposal to a white girl.

According to a dispatch from Lewisburg, Johnson had been warned several days before his death to leave the area for making "an improper proposal to a young girl of that neighborhood." The Austin Weekly Statesman's shorter version said the warning was for "insulting a young girl." The reports do not name the girl, her family or the people who delivered the warning.

Johnson's body, "riddled with bullets," was found near Farmington on August 27. The dispatch gave no witnesses, time or circumstances of the shooting, saying only that he was "supposed to have been killed by a mob."
No report of an inquest, arrest or grand jury inquiry into the killing appears in the coverage.

The news reached the press as a single brief Lewisburg telegram, which ran in dailies from Texas to New Hampshire between August 28 and 29. Editors gave it their own headlines: the Indianapolis Journal's "Negro 'Riddled' by a Mob," the Providence News's "Riddled With Bullets" and Foster's Daily Democrat's "Negro Neglected a Warning," the last placing the weight on Johnson's failure to leave. The Fort Worth Gazette and the Austin Weekly Statesman printed shorter versions that left out the mob altogether.

In the weekly news-summary columns that followed, the hedged wording disappeared. The Diamond Drill of Crystal Falls, Michigan, reported on August 31 that Johnson "(colored) was lynched by a mob for making an insulting proposal to a white girl," the first mention of the girl's race. The same sentence ran in early September in small papers in Minnesota and Wisconsin, among them the Ely Miner, the Warren Sheaf and the River Falls Journal. None of the white reports commented on the killing, and no account of it was found in the Black press.

The accounts differ on the accusation and on who killed Johnson. The original dispatch spoke of an "improper proposal to a young girl" and only supposed a mob, while the later summary called the girl white and stated that a mob lynched him. Because the summary is a rewrite of the same wire news rather than a fresh report, its firmer wording adds no independent evidence.

reader.title: Killing of Jerry Johnson
bases: A Black man who had been warned to leave over an alleged proposal to a girl was found shot to death and was 'supposed to have been killed by a mob' (A2, A3), later reported flatly as 'lynched by a mob' (A6).

Johnson was found 'riddled with bullets' after a warning to leave over an alleged improper proposal, which ties the killing to a pretext of punishing an offense (A1, A2, A3); no authority is reported, but the first wires only 'supposed' a mob and no number of killers is given, while the later summary's 'lynched by a mob' (A6) is a rewrite of the same wire news.
Every report traces to one Lewisburg wire item of Aug. 27-29 (A1-A5) and a weekly news-summary rewrite of it (A6, reprinted A7-A13); no local, Tennessee or Black-press account was found.

framing.detail: Dailies ran the Lewisburg wire as a one-paragraph brief, the Indianapolis Journal under 'Negro "Riddled" by a Mob' and Foster's under 'Negro Neglected a Warning', repeating the accusation without comment.
Weekly summary columns compressed the story into one sentence that dropped the hedge and stated he 'was lynched by a mob' for a proposal 'to a white girl'.
